demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a painter. The precision, the attention to detail, the way a room could be transformed with just the right colors – it was more than just a job, it was an expression of himself. But that all changed on the day his younger brother, Kwame, died suddenly in a tragic accident. Kofi remembered every detail of that day: the phone call from his sister-in-law, the numbness as he drove to her house, the feeling of being punched in the gut when he saw Kwame's lifeless body. It was as if time had stopped. In the months that followed, Kofi found himself struggling to focus on his work. The smell of paint and turpentine, once invigorating, now made him feel nauseous. He couldn't bear to be in his own workshop, where he and Kwame used to spend hours working on projects together. As the days turned into weeks, Kofi began to notice that certain sounds would set off a chain reaction of emotions: the wail of an ambulance siren, the chatter of people talking about losing loved ones. He'd try to shake it off, but his mind would inevitably wander back to Kwame. At night, he found himself lying awake, feeling like he was on high alert, waiting for something else to go wrong. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, even in the safety of his own home. When memories of that day did surface, Kofi felt overwhelmed by grief. Sometimes, it wasn't even a clear image or memory that triggered the emotions – just a feeling of intense sadness that seemed to come out of nowhere. He'd see flashes of Kwame's smile, hear the sound of his laughter, and be transported back to that terrible day. Kofi struggled to make sense of who he was anymore. He felt lost, isolated, like he didn't fit into his own life. His wife, Ama, tried to be supportive, but Kofi couldn't shake the feeling that she just didn't understand what he was going through. He began to withdraw from social gatherings, unable to bear the thought of being around people who seemed so carefree. As a painter, Kofi used to take pride in his ability to transform spaces, to bring new life into old rooms. Now, it felt like his own life had been destroyed by the trauma. Every day was a struggle to find meaning, to make sense of what had happened. The paint-stained overalls he once wore with such pride now hung limp and unused in his workshop. It wasn't until Ama sat him down and expressed her deep concern about the toll this was taking on their relationship that Kofi realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this, constantly on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop. What finally brought him to seek therapy was the fear of losing himself completely – and his hope that somehow, someway, he could find a way back to being the person he once was.
